overview: This file combines wartime and immediate postwar statistical material on Japan’s chemical-fertilizer industry with 1946–1947 State Department correspondence concerning mineral resources and industrial reconstruction. The fertilizer enclosures chart the sharp wartime decline in nitrogen supplies, ammonium sulfate, calcium cyanamide, and superphosphate production. Later documents address proposed private bauxite mining in the former Japanese-mandated Pacific islands, safeguards for indigenous land and resources, the unresolved trusteeship question, possible Chinese salt and Australian coal inputs for Japanese soda-ash exports, reparations policy for Japan’s aluminum industry, and a proposed investigation of Japanese sulfur deposits.

subfiles.title: Spaght transmittal of Japanese fertilizer statistics
subfiles.from: M. E. Spaght, Director, Oil and Chemical Division, United States Strategic Bombing Survey
subfiles.about: Transmits statistical tables concerning fertilizer production and supply in Japan in response to Selma G. Kallis’s request.
subfiles.summary: Spaght responds to a January 18 request sent by Selma G. Kallis to A. R. Merz for information brought back from Japan. He forwards tables on the Home Islands’ nitrogen balance, ammonia, ammonium sulfate and cyanamide production, and superphosphates. Although four enclosures are listed, only three distinct statistical tables are represented in the supplied pages.

subfiles.title: Ammonium sulfate and cyanamide production table
subfiles.from: United States Strategic Bombing Survey, Oil and Chemical Division
subfiles.about: Tabulates Japanese production, imports, exports, and monthly rates for ammonium sulfate and calcium cyanamide from 1940 through August 1945.
subfiles.summary: The table provides annual and quarterly figures for ammonium sulfate production and imports and calcium cyanamide production and exports in the Japanese Home Islands. It documents a steep decline after 1941, particularly during 1944–1945. The cited sources are the Chemical Industry Control Association and the Import-Export Bureau.

subfiles.title: Nitrogen balance in the Japanese Home Islands
subfiles.from: United States Strategic Bombing Survey, Oil and Chemical Division
subfiles.about: Presents quarterly nitrogen production, supply, consumption, and use by chemical category from 1940 through mid-1945.
subfiles.summary: The first page calculates nitrogen supply from synthetic ammonia, cyanamide, by-product ammonia, and imports. The continuation distributes consumption among civilian and Army-Navy nitric acid, ammonium sulfate, cyanamide, miscellaneous uses, and explosives or related categories. The series demonstrates the disappearance of imports and the contraction of total nitrogen supply as the war progressed.

subfiles.title: Superphosphate production and exports table
subfiles.from: United States Strategic Bombing Survey, Oil and Chemical Division
subfiles.about: Lists annual and quarterly production and export figures for superphosphate in the Japanese Home Islands from 1940 through August 1945.
subfiles.summary: The table records production falling from approximately 1.85 million short tons in 1940 to only 8,200 tons during April–August 1945. Exports similarly dwindled from 41,700 tons in 1940 to none reported in 1944–1945. Its sources are the Chemical Industry Control Association and Import Export Bureau.

subfiles.title: Martin reply opposing immediate bauxite concession
subfiles.from: Edwin M. Martin, Chief, Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs
subfiles.to: G. R. Parker, Chief, Pacific Ocean Division, U.S. Commercial Company
subfiles.about: Advises against proceeding with a private bauxite-mining concession in the Japanese Mandated Islands until their international status is clarified.
subfiles.summary: Martin answers Parker’s December 11 inquiry about private mining under an open-bid concession and Navy-imposed conditions. He explains that the United States intends to submit a strategic-trusteeship agreement for the islands to the Security Council. Because commercial policy will be part of those negotiations, the Department considers it unwise to prejudge the outcome by authorizing the concession.

subfiles.title: Parker inquiry concerning Babelthuap bauxite
subfiles.from: G. R. Parker, Chief, Pacific Ocean Division, U.S. Commercial Company
subfiles.to: John K. Emerson, Division of Japanese Affairs
subfiles.about: Requests the State Department’s view on permitting a private corporation to resume bauxite mining on Babelthuap in Palau.
subfiles.summary: Parker notes that Japan mined bauxite on Babelthuap before the war and that substantial reserves apparently remain despite wartime destruction of equipment. The Navy then exercised jurisdiction and contemplated an open-bid concession with requirements governing imported labor, housing, and related matters. Parker asks whether the State Department would object if satisfactory arrangements could be negotiated.

subfiles.title: Whitman draft approving bauxite contract conditionally
subfiles.from: Roswell M. Whitman, Associate Chief, Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs
subfiles.to: G. R. Parker, Chief, Pacific Ocean Division, U.S. Commercial Company
subfiles.about: Offers conditional State Department acceptance of an outside corporate contract for bauxite mining under military government.
subfiles.summary: The draft says the Department would probably not object to an outside corporation mining bauxite where local enterprise was not ready. It requires adequate compensation held in trust for indigenous inhabitants, protection of their land and resources, acceptable treatment of imported labor, consistency with anti-monopoly policy, and termination of the contract when military government ends. It also recommends joint Navy–State participation in setting the contract terms.

subfiles.title: Cox proposal for Japanese soda-ash raw materials
subfiles.to: Edwin M. Martin, Department of State
subfiles.about: Suggests investigating Chinese salt and Australian coal as inputs for export-oriented soda-ash production in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cox reports a possibility that northern Chinese salt and Australian coal could provide the raw materials needed for Japan to manufacture an exportable surplus of soda ash. He recommends that Martin’s office examine these supply possibilities as part of its investigation into Japanese soda-ash exports to the United States.

subfiles.title: Martin response on soda-ash investigation
subfiles.from: Edwin M. Martin, Chief, Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs
subfiles.about: Declines to have the State Department investigate the proposed Chinese and Australian raw-material arrangements for Japanese soda-ash production.
subfiles.summary: Martin acknowledges Cox’s proposal and says the Department is interested in exploring the general possibilities. He nevertheless explains that State must confine itself to policy questions rather than the details of individual commercial arrangements. Those details would have to be settled with the War Department and the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers after agreement on the proposed contract’s general form.

subfiles.title: Borton letter on Japanese aluminum reparations policy
subfiles.from: Hugh Borton, Chief, Division of Northeast Asian Affairs
subfiles.about: Summarizes the Far Eastern Commission’s May 13, 1946 policy concerning interim reparations removals from Japan’s light-metals industry.
subfiles.summary: Borton explains that alumina, aluminum, magnesium, and associated fabrication facilities were generally made available for reparations claims. Exceptions protected scrap-remelting facilities, limited equipment installed in converted cement plants, and enough general-purpose rolling and drawing machinery to fabricate 15,000 metric tons of aluminum annually. The letter presents this decision as the only information then available on the future of Japan’s aluminum industry.

subfiles.title: Kirlin routing memorandum on sulfur-deposit investigation
subfiles.from: Florence Kirlin, Office of the Secretary
subfiles.about: Requests preparation of a reply for Robert A. Lovett concerning permission for a party to investigate Japanese sulfur deposits.
subfiles.summary: Kirlin forwards the substance of a July 8 letter from Mr. Williams seeking government assistance. She asks Martin’s office to draft a response for Lovett’s signature regarding permission to send an investigating party to Japanese sulfur deposits. The Williams letter itself is not included in the supplied text.

interest: The file is valuable for linking quantitative evidence of Japan’s wartime chemical-industry collapse with the policy problems of occupation and reconstruction. Particularly revealing is the contrast between Whitman’s draft conditional approval of private bauxite mining and Martin’s later decision to defer action because of the impending trusteeship negotiations. The documents also expose competing postwar priorities: rebuilding Japanese export industries, extracting reparations, preventing monopoly, protecting indigenous Pacific land and resources, and controlling foreign corporate access. The transmittal’s reference to four tables when only three appear in the supplied pages may also help identify a missing ammonia enclosure.
